title: The ethics of making and choosing images — Image Wiki
text:
The ethics of making and choosing images
  An image can be true in every detail and still argue for something false. What that means for the person choosing the image, and for the people in it.

  
    Termimage ethics / visual ethics
    Also calledvisual ethics, photo ethics, responsible imagery, consent in photographs
    Not the same ascopyright and licensing, content moderation rules, taste
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Every image is a set of choices, including about who is in itShow your workMisleading while entirely accurateConsent and dignityWho gets a say — an argued positionCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Stand at the end of a queue of forty people and photograph along it: the line runs out of the frame and looks endless. Walk to the side and shoot across it: eight people and a lot of empty pavement. Nobody was added, nobody was removed, no pixel was altered, and the two pictures support opposite claims about how long you will be waiting.
That is the shape of almost every real problem here. Outright fakes are rare and easy to argue about. The hard cases are true. Purdue OWL puts the mechanism plainly: photographs are frames of reality, and any given subject can be photographed an infinite number of ways.
Every image is a set of choices, including about who is in it
Data Feminism's first principle is examine power, and the questions it asks of a dataset work on a picture too: who made it, who benefits from it, and who is missing.
D'Ignazio and Klein open with maternal mortality in the United States. Black women were dying in childbirth at over three times the rate of white women, community groups had said so for decades, and when journalists went looking for the numbers behind the complications, nobody was counting. As late as 2018 there was still no national system tracking complications in pregnancy and childbirth — while such systems had long existed for teen pregnancy, hip replacements and heart attacks. The CDC's William Callaghan: "What we choose to measure is a statement of what we value in health." The authors add the edit that matters — it is also a statement of who we value.

060%50%25%15%10%excludedABCDnot recorded060%24%12%7%5%52%ABCDnot recordedDenominator: rows with an answer“Half of all cases are type A”480 of the 1,000 rows countedDenominator: every row“A is 24%. We do not know about 52%.”all 1,000 rows counted

Same thousand rows, one decision. Left, the rows with no answer were dropped and the four categories were rescaled to fill the space, so A comes out at 50%. Right, the same rows counted against everybody: A is 24%, and the biggest bar in the chart is not recorded, at 52%.
Both charts are arithmetically correct. Only one of them tells you that most of this data does not exist. When you are handed a percentage, the useful question is not "is that number right" but "what is underneath the line".


Their point about the process is worth holding on to: converting a life into data always reduces it, and the reduction is where things go missing. Before there are data, there are people — and there are also, always, people who go uncounted.
Show your work
"Show your work" is Data Feminism's seventh principle, and it is narrower than it sounds: the chapter is titled Make Labor Visible, and it is about naming the hands. The Ship Map — every merchant voyage of 2012, drawn — took seventy-five researchers to assemble and validate the data, an academic team to model it, a design studio to draw it, and tens of thousands of ships to generate it. The credit usually stops at the studio. Their separate argument, that numbers do not speak for themselves and need their context supplied, is a different chapter of the same book.
Put together, the practical demand is short. Say where the image came from. Say what was done to it. Say when. Say who is not in it. Say how sure you are.
Misleading while entirely accurate
Four mechanisms cover most cases. The chart-specific versions — cut baselines, dual axes, area doing a length's job — are in When a chart lies.
A chosen frame. The queue. Nothing is added; the edge of the picture does the arguing.
An arrangement presented as a discovery.


As Gardner titled it: "A Sharpshooter's Last Sleep"
The same man, retitled: "Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter"


Alexander Gardner, Gettysburg, July 1863; both plates appear in Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the War, 1866. Library of Congress and National Archives; both public domain.
One dead man, twice. Follow the dark coat, the white cloth bunched at the chest and the head thrown back with the mouth open across both frames. On the left he lies in open ground with a rifle laid flat in front of him. On the right he is tucked into a stone barricade in Devil's Den, and a musket now stands propped against the rock — the tidy vertical that makes the composition work.
Gardner's crew carried the body about forty yards between exposures. Every grain of both negatives is a true record of light. The second title claims he was a sharpshooter, shot at his own post, and the negative cannot support that.


One example standing in for a population.


Wide: pebbles, a dry stem at the bottom edge, ground with texture
Tight: nothing in the frame but cracks


Arthur Rothstein, a steer skull in the South Dakota badlands, 1936, made for the US Resettlement Administration. Library of Congress; public domain.
The same skull, the same afternoon, two exposures — and it has been picked up and turned between them, which is why the story broke when a newspaper noticed. Look only at what the frame decides. Left, loose pebbles, a change of surface across the top, a dry stem at the bottom edge. Right, cracked alkali to every edge, and the drought is total.


An image implying a claim it does not carry. A stock photograph of a smiling nurse on a clinic page is not evidence that this clinic has nurses, and a photograph of a busy workshop above the words "made by hand in Yorkshire" asserts nothing about where anything was made. Purdue OWL's small example is a skyline with the street lights retouched out, and the question it leaves: where is the line between an accurate portrayal of reality and an aesthetic representation of it?
Consent and dignity



Jacob Riis, Lodgers in a Crowded Bayard Street Tenement, New York, c. 1889, from How the Other Half Lives. Public domain.
Riis went into lodging rooms at night and fired magnesium flash powder. The evidence is in the faces: the man in the upper bunk, propped on one elbow, looking straight down the lens with the expression of somebody who has just been woken by an explosion; the two heads at the right, half out of the blankets. They are barefoot, in bed, in a room the size of a cupboard, and they are identifiable.
The photographs helped force New York to change its housing law. Both things are true at once, and pretending otherwise is the easy way out.


The working questions are not complicated. Would this person recognise themselves? Did they agree to this use, or to being photographed at all? Does the picture show them at their worst for the benefit of somebody else's argument? Could publishing it cost them a job, a visa, a relationship?
Who gets a say — an argued position
Everything above is checkable. What follows is not a finding; it is a stance, and worth labelling as one. The Design Justice Network's principles, in their words:

We center the voices of those who are directly impacted by the outcomes of the design process.
We see the role of the designer as a facilitator rather than an expert.
We believe that everyone is an expert based on their own lived experience, and that we all have unique and brilliant contributions to bring to a design process.

Design Justice Network Principles, summer 2018, CC BY-ND 4.0.
You can disagree with that, and people do. It is not measured, it cannot be tested, and it does not tell you what to do when the affected people disagree with each other. Data Feminism is the same kind of claim: an argument about how power runs through data work, not a result. Treat both as positions taken with reasons — and say which one you are using when you defend a decision, instead of dressing it up as a rule.
Common mistakes

"Nothing was edited, so it is honest." Every mechanism above survives a forensic check. Accuracy and honesty are separate tests.
"It is representative, I have seen loads like it." Then you have a sample, not a story. Say how many and out of how many.
"They were in a public place, so consent is fine." Legality and decency are different questions, and the answer changes with what the picture is used to argue.
"Someone else's rules cover this." A guideline tells you the floor. The choice of which frame, which example and which face is still yours.


Before you approve an image

What is the claim it will be read as making? Write it in one sentence.
What is outside the frame that would weaken that claim?
Was anything arranged, moved, retouched or retimed — and would the caption still be true if you said so?
Is anyone identifiable, and would they be content to be shown like this?
If it carries numbers: what is the denominator, and who is not in it?
